Building the ground here

About this view

Mars at true scale, from the whole globe down to standing on the ground, at any place and any date. The large shapes and colours come from spacecraft maps. Detail smaller than those maps is made by rule and is not a record of the real ground.

From real data

  • Heights: the Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) gridded topography, 4 pixels per degree, about 15 km per pixel. NASA Goddard MOLA team, via the PDS Geosciences Node.
  • Colour: the Viking orbiter colour mosaic (NASA, JPL, USGS), 1440 by 720, from NASA's 3D Resources. Phobos and Deimos maps from the same collection.
  • Place names: the IAU Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature (USGS), from a copy made some years ago, so recent names may be missing. Landing sites from NASA, USGS and mission papers.
  • Sun and local time: the Mars24 algorithm of NASA GISS (Allison and McEwen, 2000). Mars' pole and spin: IAU working group values (2009).
  • Earth, Venus, Jupiter and Saturn in the sky: JPL's approximate planet positions. About sixty bright stars at their catalogue positions, rounded.
  • Phobos and Deimos: sizes from ESA; orbits from JPL mean elements. Phobos rises in the west and crosses the sky in about four hours; Deimos rises in the east and takes days.
  • Gravity 3.71 m/s², mean radius 3,389.5 km, a sol of 24 h 39 min 35 s, axis tilted 25.19°, from NASA and ESA fact sheets.

Made by rule, or set by eye

  • Craters smaller than about 10 km, hills, dunes, rocks, pebbles and ripples. They follow simple rules: more craters on the old southern highlands, fewer on the volcanoes and polar layers, dunes in dark low ground.
  • How the dust colours the light: it lets blue light through near the sun, which is why sunsets are blue, and scatters red and yellow across the rest of the sky. The amounts are set by eye to match rover photographs.
  • Where and when clouds form: thin water-ice clouds in the belt near the equator in northern spring and summer, polar hoods in each hemisphere's autumn and winter, clouds over the great volcanoes in the afternoon, and high carbon-dioxide clouds that shine with colour after sunset early in southern autumn. The pattern is a simple model.
  • The edge of the seasonal frost cap, the fainter stars and the texture of the Milky Way (its band is in its true place).
  • Moon positions are good to a few degrees, not an exact ephemeris. At night the moons are shown as a dark-adapted eye would see them.
